card.title: Gas Laws: Boyle's, Charles', Avogadro's, Combined Gas Equation, Dalton's Law of Partial Pressure and Graham's Law of Diffusion

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Five laws, one toolkit. **Boyle** (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂) compresses isothermally — 3 atm on 2 L relaxes to 6 L at 1 atm. **Charles** (V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂) demands Kelvin: 500 cm³ at 300 K swells to 666.7 cm³ at 400 K, and every gas extrapolates to nothing at −273.15 °C. **Avogadro** equalises molecules per litre (22.4 L at STP).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂; P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ - P(total) = p₁ + p₂ + …; P(dry) = P(wet) − aqueous tension - r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁); t₁/t₂ = √(M₁/M₂) - Molar volume at STP = 22.4 L

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **STP means 0 °C and 1 atm** (molar volume 22.4 L) — not room temperature; quoting 24 L at "STP" confuses NTP/room conditions.  ·  **Boyle's law needs constant temperature, Charles's needs constant pressure:** mixing the constraints (or forgetting which variable is held) derails the choice of equation.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The total pressure exerted by a mixture of non-reacting gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures which each gas would exert if it alone occupied the whole volume."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The rising dough of bread*** — CO₂ from yeast obeys Charles's law: oven heat expands each bubble in exact T proportion, doubling the dough's gas volume from 30 °C to 180 °C... wait — from 303 K to 453 K, a 1.5× lift.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: gas laws, boyle's law, charles' law, avogadro's law (within States of Matter).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Four Laws, One Gas Boyle, Charles, Avogadro, Dalton and Graham each measured one slice of gas behaviour; together they form the toolkit for every gas numerical. This topic carries the heaviest PYQ load in the unit — a 2024 set alone tested Boyle's law, Graham's law, and Dalton's law with aqueous tension — so the worked numericals below are the exam's own patterns.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Boyle's law (T, n constant) - **V ∝ 1/P**, or **P₁V₁ = P₂V₂** — doubling the pressure halves the volume. - Graph: P vs V is a hyperbola; PV = constant is a straight horizontal line. ### 2.2 Charles's law (P, n constant) - **V ∝ T (absolute)**, or **V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂** — every gas extrapolates to zero volume at −273.15 °C, the origin of the absolute scale.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Kelvin before anything". Boyle: multiply, divide (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂). Graham: heavier is slower; square both sides. Over water: subtract aqueous tension. STP = 0 °C, 1 atm, 22.4 L.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB 2024 (2m): 2 L of a gas at 3 atm pressure expands isothermally. What volume will it occupy at 1 atm?** — Isothermal means temperature is constant, so **Boyle's law** applies: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. Substituting: 3 atm × 2 L = 1 atm × V₂, giving V₂ = 6/1 = **6 L**.…  ·  **NEB 2021 (2m): A sample of gas occupies 500 cm³ at 27 °C and 1 atm. Calculate the volume at 127 °C at the same pressure.** — Convert temperatures to Kelvin first: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T₂ = 127 + 273 = 400 K. Pressure is constant, so **Charles's law** applies: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: State the law in words before the equation — both carry marks. For Graham's numericals, show the squaring step; for aqueous tension, name the temperature at which the tension applies.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: All four partial laws are special cases of PV = nRT (topic 45); recognising which variables are constant in a problem selects the right law instantly.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (T, n fixed; hyperbola). Charles: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ (Kelvin!; extrapolates to −273.15 °C). Avogadro: V ∝ n; 22.4 L/mol at STP. Combined: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. Dalton: P = p₁ + p₂ + …; aqueous tension subtracted for gas over water. Graham: r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁); H₂ 4× faster than M = 32 gas.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Airplane cabins are pressurised to about 0.75 atm — Boyle's law sets how much air passengers carry per breath, and Dalton's law says the oxygen share of that thinner air is what matters.

Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Verified PYQ (NEB 2024): Boyle's law numerical — 2 L at 3 atm expands to 1 atm - Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → 3 × 2 = 1 × V₂ → **V₂ = 6 L** (isothermal expansion). ### 4.2 Verified PYQ (NEB 2021): combined law — 500 cm³ at 27 °C to 127 °C - Kelvin first: 300 K → 400 K. V₂ = V₁T₂/T₁ = 500 × 400/300 = **666.7 cm³** (pressure constant per the question).…  ·  ### Deep dive — the gas laws as one connected story Each gas law isolates **two** of the four variables P, V, n, T and holds the other two fixed; the combined gas equation and PV = nRT are just the laws multiplied together. Boyle (P ∝ 1/V at fixed n, T) is the compression story — doubling P halves V because the same number of molecules now strike the walls twice as often.…

rows.text: Verified PYQs: NEB 2024 — Graham's law numerical (M = 32), Dalton's law with aqueous tension, Boyle's 2 L/3 atm numerical; NEB 2021 — combined-law 500 cm³ → 666.7 cm³; NEB 2023 — Boyle + Charles with derivation of the ideal gas equation (solved in topic 45). rows.text: A gas collected over water at 25 °C reads 745 mmHg (aqueous tension 23.8 mmHg); find the dry gas pressure.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  Limit to remember: ideal gas equation pv = nrt; from kinetic theory p = ⅓ (nm/m)⟨c²⟩, so pv = ⅓n m⟨c²⟩.

Common Confusions **Celsius must become Kelvin before any gas-law algebra:** using 27 °C directly in Charles's law gives nonsense; add 273 first — the single most common numerical error.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Aqueous tension is subtracted, not the other way:** the water vapour adds pressure to the wet gas; the dry gas's share is what remains.  ·  **Diffusion rate ratios invert with molar mass:** the lighter gas is faster — writing r ∝ √M reverses the law.  ·  ## 7. Exam Application **Verified PYQ (NEB 2024): State Graham's law. Hydrogen diffuses 4 times faster than an unknown gas; find its molar mass.** — Graham's law: at constant temperature and pressure, the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass; r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁).…
